slides.narration: Namaste! Iron in bridges, copper in wires, titanium in aircraft, chromium on taps and platinum in car exhausts: the metals in the middle of the periodic table build the modern world. These are the d-block elements, and below the main table sit the f-block elements. In this part we study their electronic configurations and the special properties that come from partly filled d orbitals.

slides.heading: Where are the d- and f-block elements?
slides.body_md: The **d-block** fills groups 3–12 in periods 4–7, giving the **3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series**. A **transition element** has an **incompletely filled d subshell** in the atom or in one of its common ions. Zinc, cadmium and mercury have full $d^{10}$ shells in the atom and in their common ions, so they are not regarded as transition elements, though they are d-block elements.

visual.alt: Table of the four d-series with their period, first and last elements and the d orbitals being filled

slides.narration: The d-block sits between the s-block and the p-block, in groups three to twelve. Each period from four to seven gives one series. A transition element is defined by an incomplete d subshell, either in the atom or in a common ion. Copper counts, because its common ion has nine d electrons. Zinc does not, because both the atom and its ion have a full set of ten.

slides.heading: Electronic configurations of the 3d series
slides.body_md: General configuration: $(n-1)d^{1\text{–}10}\, ns^{1\text{–}2}$. Chromium and copper are exceptions: a **half-filled** ($d^5$) or **completely filled** ($d^{10}$) d subshell has extra stability, and the 3d and 4s energies are very close.

visual.alt: Table of the electronic configurations of the 3d elements from scandium to zinc, with chromium 3d5 4s1 and copper 3d10 4s1

slides.narration: Across the three d series, electrons go into the three d orbitals while the four s holds one or two. Two elements break the simple pattern. Chromium is three d five, four s one, not three d four, four s two; copper is three d ten, four s one. A half-filled or completely filled d subshell is especially stable, and because three d and four s are so close in energy, one electron shifts to achieve it.

slides.heading: Worked example: configurations of ions
slides.body_md:
**Rule.** When a 3d atom forms a cation, the **4s electrons are removed first**, then 3d.

**Problem.** Write the configurations of $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $\ce{Cu+}$ and $\ce{Mn^2+}$ (Fe = 26, Cu = 29, Mn = 25).

**Step 1.** Fe $[\text{Ar}]3d^6 4s^2$ → $\ce{Fe^2+}$ $[\text{Ar}]3d^6$ → $\ce{Fe^3+}$ $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$.

**Step 2.** Cu $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10} 4s^1$ → $\ce{Cu+}$ $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$; Mn $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^2$ → $\ce{Mn^2+}$ $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$.

visual.alt: Table of the configurations and numbers of unpaired electrons of iron two plus, iron three plus, copper one plus and manganese two plus

slides.narration: The rule that trips up many students: the four s electrons leave first, even though they went in first. Iron loses its two four s electrons to become iron two plus, three d six, and then one three d electron to become iron three plus, three d five. Copper one plus is three d ten. Manganese two plus is three d five, a half-filled set with five unpaired electrons.

slides.heading: Quick check: configuration of an ion
slides.body_md: Choose the correct configuration of a 3d ion, remembering which electrons are removed first.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the atom’s configuration first, then remove the four s electrons before touching the three d electrons.

slides.heading: Physical properties and metallic bonding
slides.body_md: Transition metals are hard, dense, lustrous and good conductors, with high melting points (except zinc, cadmium and mercury). **Unpaired d electrons take part in metallic bonding**, so bonding is strongest, and the **enthalpy of atomisation** highest, near the middle of each series.

rows: Rises to a maximum near V–Cr, then falls; Zn lowest
More unpaired d electrons, stronger metallic bonding
Full d¹⁰: d electrons not used in bonding

visual.alt: Table of trends in melting point, enthalpy of atomisation and hardness across the 3d series, with zinc, cadmium and mercury as exceptions

slides.narration: Why are transition metals so hard and strong? Besides the outer s electrons, their unpaired d electrons join in the metallic bonding. More unpaired electrons means stronger bonding, so melting points and enthalpies of atomisation rise towards the middle of the series and then fall. Zinc, cadmium and mercury, with full d subshells, have weak metallic bonding; mercury is even a liquid.

slides.heading: Atomic radius across the 3d series
slides.body_md: Radii fall quickly at the start of the series, then stay **almost constant**: each added electron goes into the inner 3d subshell, whose **poor shielding** is balanced by **repulsion** between d electrons. Similar sizes let transition metals form **alloys** easily.

visual.alt: Metallic radii of the 3d series from scandium to zinc: a sharp fall from 164 picometres at scandium to about 129 at chromium, then nearly constant around 125 to 137 in the middle and end of the series
visual.caption: Approximate values. Radii fall at first, then stay almost constant because added 3d electrons shield the outer electrons poorly but also repel one another.

slides.narration: Across the 3d series the nuclear charge rises by one each time, but the new electron goes into an inner d orbital, not the outer shell. At first the radius shrinks quickly, from scandium to chromium. After that, the extra pull is balanced by repulsion between the growing number of d electrons, so the radius hardly changes. Atoms of similar size can replace each other in a metal lattice, which is why these metals form so many alloys.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: First ionisation enthalpies rise only slowly and irregularly across the series, because the shielding by added 3d electrons almost balances the extra nuclear charge. Some **second ionisation enthalpies are unusually high**: removing the second electron from $\ce{Cr+}$ ($3d^5$) or $\ce{Cu+}$ ($3d^{10}$) breaks a stable configuration.

rows: Small, irregular rise in first IE
Shielding by 3d electrons nearly cancels the rise in nuclear charge
High second IE of Cr and Cu
Breaks the stable d⁵ or d¹⁰ configuration of the M⁺ ion
Removing it gives the stable d⁵ Fe³⁺
High third IE of Mn and Zn

visual.alt: Table of observations about ionisation enthalpies in the 3d series and their reasons, based on the stability of d5 and d10 configurations

slides.narration: Ionisation enthalpies of the 3d metals rise only a little across the series, and not smoothly. The useful idea is again the stability of half-filled and filled d subshells. Pulling the second electron out of chromium one plus or copper one plus destroys a stable set, so it costs a lot. Pulling a third electron out of manganese two plus, which is d five, is also unusually hard.

slides.heading: Variable oxidation states
slides.body_md: Because 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies, transition elements show **several oxidation states**, usually differing by one. The number rises to a maximum at **manganese (+7)**, then falls. Higher states are found in oxides and fluorides; low states in complexes with ligands such as CO.

visual.alt: Table of the common and highest oxidation states of the 3d elements, rising to plus 7 at manganese and then falling

slides.narration: Iron can be iron two or iron three; manganese can range from plus two to plus seven. Because the three d and four s electrons are close in energy, different numbers of them can be used in bonding. Up to manganese, the highest state equals the total number of three d and four s electrons. After manganese, pairing makes the electrons harder to use, and the highest states fall again.

slides.heading: Standard electrode potentials of the 3d metals
slides.body_md: $E^\circ(\ce{M^2+/M})$ values reflect the energy needed to atomise and ionise the metal and the hydration energy of the ion. Copper alone has a **positive** value, so it does **not** release hydrogen from dilute acids.

visual.alt: Table of standard electrode potentials of the 3d metals for the M2+/M couples and some M3+/M2+ couples

slides.narration: The electrode potentials of the three d metals are mostly negative, so most of these metals release hydrogen from acids. Copper is the exception, with a positive value: the energy needed to turn copper metal into hydrated ions is not paid back by hydration. Notice also the large positive values for manganese three plus and cobalt three plus going to the two plus ions: those three plus ions are strong oxidising agents.

slides.heading: Worked example: why Cr²⁺ reduces and Mn³⁺ oxidises
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Both $\ce{Cr^2+}$ and $\ce{Mn^3+}$ are $d^4$ ions. Why is $\ce{Cr^2+}$ a reducing agent while $\ce{Mn^3+}$ is an oxidising agent?

**Step 1.** $\ce{Cr^2+ -> Cr^3+ + e-}$ gives $d^3$, a stable configuration with three half-filled $t_{2g}$ orbitals; $E^\circ(\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+}) = -0.41\ \text{V}$, so $\ce{Cr^2+}$ readily gives an electron.

**Step 2.** $\ce{Mn^3+ + e- -> Mn^2+}$ gives the extra-stable half-filled $d^5$; $E^\circ(\ce{Mn^3+/Mn^2+}) = +1.57\ \text{V}$, so $\ce{Mn^3+}$ readily takes an electron.

nodes.label: loses e⁻ → Cr³⁺ (d³, stable): reducing agent
gains e⁻ → Mn²⁺ (d⁵, stable): oxidising agent

visual.alt: Flow: chromium two plus loses an electron to become stable chromium three plus, so it reduces; manganese three plus gains an electron to become stable manganese two plus, so it oxidises

slides.narration: Here is a favourite reasoning question. Both ions have four d electrons, yet they behave oppositely. Chromium two plus gets to a more stable arrangement by losing an electron, so it gives electrons away: it is a reducing agent. Manganese three plus gets to the half-filled d five arrangement by gaining an electron, so it takes electrons: it is an oxidising agent. The electrode potentials confirm both.

slides.heading: Quick check: highest oxidation state
slides.body_md: Decide which 3d element shows the highest oxidation state.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count three d plus four s electrons along the series, and remember where the maximum oxidation state occurs.

slides.heading: Magnetic properties
slides.body_md: Ions with **unpaired electrons** are **paramagnetic** (attracted by a magnet); those with all electrons paired are **diamagnetic**. The **spin-only magnetic moment**, in Bohr magnetons (BM), depends on the number of unpaired electrons $n$:

visual.alt: Table of spin-only magnetic moments for zero to five unpaired electrons with example ions

slides.narration: Each unpaired electron behaves like a tiny magnet. Ions with unpaired electrons are drawn into a magnetic field: they are paramagnetic. The spin-only formula gives the magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons as the square root of n times n plus two, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. So a measured moment tells us how many unpaired electrons an ion has.

slides.heading: Worked example: magnetic moment of an ion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of $\ce{Fe^2+}$ (Fe = 26) and of $\ce{Cu^2+}$ (Cu = 29).

**Step 1.** $\ce{Fe^2+}$ is $3d^6$: five orbitals, one paired and four single, so $n = 4$: $\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\ \text{BM}$.

**Step 2.** $\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $3d^9$: $n = 1$, $\mu = \sqrt{1 \times 3} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\ \text{BM}$.

visual.alt: Table of iron two plus with six d electrons, four unpaired, 4.90 Bohr magnetons, and copper two plus with nine, one unpaired, 1.73

slides.narration: First find the d count of the ion, then the number of unpaired electrons by filling five d orbitals singly before pairing. Iron two plus has six d electrons: five go in singly and one pairs up, leaving four unpaired, so the moment is the square root of twenty four, about four point nine. Copper two plus, with nine, has just one unpaired electron, about one point seven three.

slides.heading: Colour of transition metal ions
slides.body_md: In a complex or hydrated ion, the five d orbitals split into groups of slightly different energy. An electron can jump between them (**d–d transition**) by absorbing part of visible light; the ion shows the **complementary colour**. Ions with $d^0$ or $d^{10}$ configurations are colourless.

visual.alt: Table of colours of hydrated 3d ions from colourless scandium three plus through purple, green, violet, pink and blue to colourless zinc two plus

slides.narration: Why is copper sulfate solution blue? In the hydrated copper ion the d orbitals are split slightly in energy. A d electron absorbs orange-red light to jump up, and we see what is left: blue. Ions with no d electrons, like scandium three plus, or a full set, like zinc two plus, have no such jump available, so their solutions are colourless.

slides.heading: Complexes, catalysts, interstitial compounds and alloys
slides.body_md: Transition metals form many **complexes** (small, highly charged ions with vacant d orbitals). They are good **catalysts**, using variable oxidation states and their surfaces. They trap small atoms (H, C, N) in their lattices as **interstitial compounds**, and form **alloys** because their atoms are similar in size.

rows: Iron in the Haber process; V₂O₅ in the contact process; nickel in hydrogenation of oils
Small atoms in lattice holes; hard, high melting, chemically inert
Small, charged ions with vacant d orbitals

visual.alt: Table of examples and reasons for catalytic activity, interstitial compounds, alloys and complex formation by transition metals

slides.narration: Transition metals are the world’s favourite catalysts: iron in ammonia manufacture, vanadium pentoxide in sulfuric acid manufacture and nickel in making vanaspati from oils. They can switch between oxidation states and hold reactant molecules on their surfaces. Small atoms like carbon and nitrogen fit into the gaps of their lattices, giving very hard interstitial compounds. And similar atomic sizes make alloys such as brass and stainless steel easy to form.

slides.heading: Quick check: colour and magnetism
slides.body_md: Pick the ion that is both colourless and diamagnetic.
slides.narration: Quick check. Both properties need the same thing: think about which d configurations leave no unpaired electron and no possible d–d jump.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Transition element: incomplete d subshell in the atom or a common ion; Zn, Cd, Hg are d-block but not transition elements.
3d configurations $3d^{1\text{–}10}4s^{1\text{–}2}$; Cr $3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu $3d^{10} 4s^1$; ions lose 4s electrons first.
Radii fall then level off; melting point and atomisation enthalpy peak mid-series.
Oxidation states vary, maximum +7 at Mn; stability of d⁵ and d¹⁰ explains many E° and IE anomalies.
$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM; colour from d–d transitions; $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless.
Catalysts, interstitial compounds, alloys and complexes are typical of transition metals.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas for configuration, oxidation states, magnetism and colour

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Transition elements have incomplete d subshells. Chromium and copper have special configurations, and ions lose their four s electrons first. The extra stability of half-filled and filled d subshells explains many trends in ionisation enthalpy, oxidation state and electrode potential. Unpaired d electrons give magnetism and colour, and these metals are excellent catalysts and form alloys and interstitial compounds.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: For ions, remove 4s electrons before 3d: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶, not 3d⁴4s².
Count unpaired electrons by filling five d orbitals singly first.
Give the reason with every anomaly: half-filled d⁵ or filled d¹⁰ stability.
Zinc is not a transition element: say why (d¹⁰ in atom and ion).
For colour, mention d–d transition and absorption of visible light; for magnetism, unpaired electrons.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. When writing ions, take electrons from four s first. When counting unpaired electrons, fill all five d orbitals singly before pairing. Every anomaly answer should mention the special stability of half-filled or filled d subshells. Explain why zinc is not a transition element. And for colour, always mention d to d transitions and the absorption of visible light.

slides.narration: In Part 2 we meet two compounds you will use in the practical laboratory: orange potassium dichromate and deep purple potassium permanganate. Both are powerful oxidising agents. Then we move to the f-block: the lanthanoids, whose steadily shrinking size has surprising consequences, and the actinoids, which include uranium and plutonium. We finish with uses of these elements in everyday life and industry.

slides.heading: Making potassium dichromate
slides.body_md: From **chromite ore** ($\ce{FeCr2O4}$): (1) fuse with sodium carbonate in air to give sodium chromate; (2) acidify to give sodium dichromate; (3) add potassium chloride; the less soluble potassium dichromate crystallises.

nodes.label: Fuse with Na₂CO₃ in air → Na₂CrO₄ (yellow)

visual.alt: Flow for making potassium dichromate: chromite ore fused with sodium carbonate in air to sodium chromate, acidified to sodium dichromate, then potassium chloride added

slides.narration: Potassium dichromate is made from chromite, an ore of iron and chromium. Heating the ore with sodium carbonate in air oxidises chromium to yellow sodium chromate. Adding acid turns the chromate into orange dichromate. Finally, potassium chloride is added: potassium dichromate is less soluble than the sodium salt, so it crystallises out as orange crystals.

slides.heading: Chromate and dichromate: structures and pH
slides.body_md: Chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing a corner oxygen. They interconvert with pH: acid turns **yellow chromate into orange dichromate**; alkali does the reverse. Chromium is **+6** in both.

slides.narration: Look at the shapes. The chromate ion is a tetrahedron of four oxygen atoms around chromium. In dichromate, two such tetrahedra share one corner oxygen. In solution the two ions are in equilibrium. Add acid, and yellow chromate turns orange as dichromate forms; add alkali, and the orange turns yellow again. Chromium is in the plus six state in both, so this is not a redox change.

slides.heading: Dichromate as an oxidising agent
slides.body_md: In acid, dichromate is a strong oxidising agent ($E^\circ = +1.33\ \text{V}$). Each dichromate ion accepts **six electrons**, and orange $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$ becomes green $\ce{Cr^3+}$.

visual.alt: Table of the ionic equations for acidified dichromate oxidising iron two, iodide, hydrogen sulfide and tin two

slides.narration: Acidified dichromate grabs six electrons per ion, and each chromium drops from plus six to plus three, turning the solution from orange to green. It oxidises iron two plus to iron three plus, iodide to iodine, hydrogen sulfide to sulfur and tin two plus to tin four plus. The colour change from orange to green was used in early breath tests for alcohol.

slides.heading: Worked example: a dichromate titration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.020\ \text{M}$ potassium dichromate exactly oxidises the iron(II) in a sample. How many moles of $\ce{Fe^2+}$ were present?

**Step 1.** Moles of dichromate $= 0.020 \times 0.0250 = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}$.

**Step 2.** From the equation, $1\ \ce{Cr2O7^2-}$ reacts with $6\ \ce{Fe^2+}$: moles of $\ce{Fe^2+} = 6 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-4} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}$.

**Step 3.** Mass of iron $= 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 56 = 0.168\ \text{g}$.

visual.alt: Table of the titration results: moles of dichromate, the 1 to 6 ratio and moles and mass of iron two

slides.narration: In titrations, the balanced ionic equation is everything. First find the moles of dichromate from its volume in litres and molarity: five ten-thousandths of a mole. The equation shows that each dichromate oxidises six iron two plus ions, so there were three thousandths of a mole of iron, or about one hundred and sixty eight milligrams.

slides.heading: Making potassium permanganate
slides.body_md: **Pyrolusite** ($\ce{MnO2}$) is fused with potassium hydroxide and an oxidant (air or potassium nitrate) to give dark green **potassium manganate**. In neutral or acid solution, manganate **disproportionates** to permanganate and $\ce{MnO2}$; industrially it is oxidised electrolytically.

nodes.label: Fuse with KOH + O₂ → K₂MnO₄ (green, Mn +6)

visual.alt: Flow for making potassium permanganate from pyrolusite through green potassium manganate

slides.narration: Potassium permanganate starts from pyrolusite, manganese dioxide. Fusing it with potassium hydroxide in air gives dark green potassium manganate, with manganese in the plus six state. In acid, manganate disproportionates: some manganese goes up to plus seven as purple permanganate, and some goes down to plus four as manganese dioxide. Industry instead oxidises manganate electrolytically, wasting none of it.

slides.heading: Manganate and permanganate
slides.body_md: Both ions are tetrahedral. **Manganate** ($\ce{MnO4^2-}$, Mn +6, $d^1$) is green and paramagnetic; **permanganate** ($\ce{MnO4-}$, Mn +7, $d^0$) is purple and diamagnetic. The intense purple comes from charge transfer, not a d–d transition.

slides.narration: Manganate and permanganate look alike: four oxygen atoms around manganese, arranged tetrahedrally. The difference is one electron. Manganate has one d electron, so it is paramagnetic and green. Permanganate has none, so it is diamagnetic. Its deep purple colour cannot come from a d to d jump; instead, light moves charge from oxygen to manganese, which is called charge transfer.

slides.heading: Permanganate as an oxidising agent
slides.body_md: In **acid**, each permanganate gains **five** electrons and becomes nearly colourless $\ce{Mn^2+}$ ($E^\circ = +1.52\ \text{V}$); this is why it acts as its own indicator in titrations. In **neutral or faintly alkaline** solution it gains **three** electrons and gives brown $\ce{MnO2}$.

visual.alt: Table of ionic equations for acidified permanganate oxidising iron two, oxalate and iodide

slides.narration: Permanganate is even more powerful than dichromate. In acid each ion takes five electrons and becomes the almost colourless manganese two plus ion. So in a titration the first extra drop leaves a permanent pink colour, and no other indicator is needed. In neutral solution it takes only three electrons and gives a brown precipitate of manganese dioxide. Hydrochloric acid is never used to acidify it, because chloride would be oxidised.

slides.heading: Worked example: a permanganate titration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What volume of $0.020\ \text{M}$ $\ce{KMnO4}$ is needed to oxidise $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.10\ \text{M}$ iron(II) sulfate in acid?

**Step 1.** Moles of $\ce{Fe^2+} = 0.10 \times 0.0250 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$.

**Step 2.** $1\ \ce{MnO4-}$ oxidises $5\ \ce{Fe^2+}$: moles of $\ce{MnO4-} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-3}}{5} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}$.

**Step 3.** Volume $= \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.020} = 0.025\ \text{L} = 25.0\ \text{mL}$.

visual.alt: Table of the permanganate titration: moles of iron two, the 1 to 5 ratio, moles of permanganate and the volume of 25.0 millilitres

slides.narration: Start from the solution you know completely: twenty five millilitres of zero point one molar iron two plus is two and a half thousandths of a mole. One permanganate ion oxidises five iron ions, so we need one fifth as many moles of permanganate. Dividing by its molarity gives twenty five millilitres. In the laboratory, the end point is the first permanent pale pink.

slides.heading: The f-block: lanthanoids and actinoids
slides.body_md: The **lanthanoids** (Ce to Lu, after La) fill the 4f orbitals; the **actinoids** (Th to Lr, after Ac) fill 5f. Together they are the **inner transition elements**. The common oxidation state of lanthanoids is **+3**; Ce⁴⁺ is a good oxidant and Eu²⁺ and Yb²⁺ are reductants, because of empty, half-filled or full f subshells.

visual.alt: Table of lanthanoid ions in unusual oxidation states, cerium four plus, europium two plus, terbium four plus and ytterbium two plus, and their configurations

slides.narration: The f-block elements are placed below the main table. In the lanthanoids, electrons fill the four f orbitals, buried deep inside the atom; in the actinoids they fill five f. Lanthanoids are mostly plus three. A few show plus two or plus four when that gives an empty, half-filled or full f subshell: cerium four plus is an oxidising agent, europium two plus a reducing agent.

slides.heading: The lanthanoid contraction
slides.body_md: From lanthanum to lutetium, atomic and ionic radii **decrease steadily**. Each added electron goes into the **4f** subshell, which shields the outer electrons very poorly from the rising nuclear charge.

visual.alt: Radius of the tripositive lanthanoid ions falling steadily from about 103 picometres for lanthanum to about 86 for lutetium
visual.caption: Approximate values: the steady decrease is the lanthanoid contraction.

slides.narration: Across the lanthanoids, the size of the tripositive ion shrinks steadily, from about one hundred and three picometres for lanthanum to about eighty six for lutetium. This is the lanthanoid contraction. The four f electrons are spread out awkwardly and shield the outer electrons poorly, so as protons are added, the outer shell is pulled in a little more each time.

slides.heading: Consequences of the lanthanoid contraction
slides.body_md: The contraction cancels the size increase expected from the 4d to the 5d series, so **second and third series elements in a group have almost equal radii** and very similar properties.

rows: 4d and 5d elements of a group are almost the same size
They occur together and are very hard to separate
Basicity of hydroxides decreases from La to Lu
Lanthanoids are hard to separate from one another
Need ion exchange or repeated crystallisation

visual.alt: Table of the consequences of the lanthanoid contraction: equal sizes of zirconium and hafnium, difficulty of separation and the fall in basicity of lanthanoid hydroxides

slides.narration: The lanthanoid contraction has surprising effects outside the f-block. Normally atoms grow down a group, but hafnium, which comes just after the lanthanoids, is almost exactly the same size as zirconium above it. So the two have nearly identical chemistry, occur together in nature and are very hard to separate. Within the series, the smaller ions hold hydroxide more tightly, so the hydroxides become less basic.

slides.heading: Lanthanoids and actinoids compared
slides.body_md: Both fill f orbitals and show a contraction, but the **5f orbitals are less deeply buried** than 4f, so actinoids are more varied.
columns:
**Lanthanoids (4f)**

- Mostly +3; a few +2 and +4
- Mostly not radioactive (except promethium)
- Contraction smaller
- Less tendency to form complexes

**Actinoids (5f)**

- Many states, up to +7 (e.g. Np, Pu)
- All radioactive; many made artificially
- Contraction greater (poorer 5f shielding)
- Greater tendency to form complexes; e.g. uranyl ion

visual.alt: Table comparing lanthanoids and actinoids by orbitals filled, oxidation states, radioactivity and complex formation

slides.narration: Lanthanoids and actinoids are cousins, but the actinoids are more adventurous. Their five f orbitals reach further out and are closer in energy to the six d and seven s orbitals, so many more electrons can be used in bonding, giving oxidation states up to plus seven. All actinoids are radioactive, and those after uranium are mostly made in nuclear reactors. They also form complexes more readily.

slides.heading: Uses of d- and f-block elements
slides.body_md: From kitchens to space, these elements are everywhere.

rows: Steels and stainless steel for construction, tools and utensils
Light, strong, corrosion-resistant parts for aircraft and implants
Catalysts for sulfuric acid, ammonia and hydrogenation of oils
Flints for lighters; alloy for steel
Phosphors in screens and LED lamps

visual.alt: Table of uses of d- and f-block elements: steels, titanium alloys, catalysts, coinage metals, silver bromide, mischmetall, lanthanoid phosphors and nuclear fuels

slides.narration: The uses are endless. Iron, chromium and nickel give us stainless steel utensils. Titanium makes light, strong aircraft parts and hip implants. Vanadium pentoxide, iron and nickel are industrial catalysts. Copper, silver and gold carry electricity and make jewellery. Mischmetall, mostly lanthanoids with some iron, makes lighter flints. Lanthanoid compounds glow in screens and lamps, and uranium fuels nuclear power stations.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Potassium dichromate and permanganate are made from their ores through chromate and manganate, and both are strong oxidising agents in acid, taking six and five electrons per ion. Mole ratios from their ionic equations drive every titration calculation. In the f-block, the lanthanoid contraction makes heavy transition metals almost the same size as those above them, and actinoids show a wider range of chemistry.

sections.heading: 1. Position and electronic configuration
sections.body_md:
The **d-block** occupies groups 3–12; its four series (3d, 4d, 5d, 6d) lie in periods 4–7. A **transition element** has an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in any of its common oxidation states; so Cu ($\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $3d^9$) is a transition element, while Zn, Cd and Hg ($d^{10}$ in atom and ion) are not.

General configuration $(n-1)d^{1\text{–}10}ns^{1\text{–}2}$. Because 3d and 4s energies are close and half-filled/filled d subshells are extra stable, **Cr is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$** and **Cu is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1$**. On ionisation, **4s electrons are removed before 3d**: $\ce{Fe^2+}$ $3d^6$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$ $3d^5$, $\ce{Mn^2+}$ $3d^5$, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ $3d^9$.

The **f-block** (lanthanoids and actinoids) is placed separately below the table; these are the **inner transition elements**.

sections.heading: 2. General properties of transition elements
sections.body_md:
- **Physical:** hard, dense, high melting points (except Zn, Cd, Hg); unpaired d electrons strengthen metallic bonding, so melting point and enthalpy of atomisation peak mid-series.
- **Radii:** fall at first, then nearly constant across a series (poor shielding by 3d balanced by d–d repulsion); 4d and 5d radii almost equal (lanthanoid contraction).
- **Ionisation enthalpy:** rises slowly and irregularly; high second IE for Cr and Cu (stable $d^5$, $d^{10}$ of $\ce{M+}$).
- **Oxidation states:** variable, usually differing by one; maximum +7 at Mn; high states in oxides/fluorides.
- **E° values:** $E^\circ(\ce{M^2+/M})$ negative except Cu (+0.34 V): copper does not displace hydrogen from dilute acids. $\ce{Mn^3+}$ ($E^\circ$ +1.57 V) and $\ce{Co^3+}$ (+1.97 V) are strong oxidants; $\ce{Cr^2+}$ ($E^\circ(\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+}) = -0.41$ V) is a reductant.
- **Magnetism:** paramagnetic if unpaired electrons; spin-only $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM.
- **Colour:** d–d transitions absorb visible light; $d^0$ ($\ce{Sc^3+}$, $\ce{Ti^4+}$) and $d^{10}$ ($\ce{Zn^2+}$, $\ce{Cu+}$) ions are colourless.
- **Catalysis:** variable oxidation states and surface adsorption (Fe in the Haber process, $\ce{V2O5}$ in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation).
- **Interstitial compounds:** small atoms (H, C, N) in lattice holes, e.g. TiC, $\ce{Mn4N}$, $\ce{Fe3H}$: hard, high melting, chemically inert, metallic conductivity.
- **Alloys:** similar atomic radii allow substitution (brass, bronze, stainless steel). **Complexes:** small, highly charged ions with vacant d orbitals.

sections.heading: 3. Potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate
sections.body_md:
**K₂Cr₂O₇ preparation:** $\ce{4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2}$; $\ce{2Na2CrO4 + 2H+ -> Na2Cr2O7 + 2Na+ + H2O}$; $\ce{Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl -> K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl}$. Chromate (yellow, tetrahedral) and dichromate (orange, two tetrahedra sharing an O) interconvert with pH; Cr is +6 in both.

**Oxidising action (acid):** $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$ ($E^\circ$ +1.33 V): oxidises $\ce{Fe^2+}$ to $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $\ce{I-}$ to $\ce{I2}$, $\ce{H2S}$ to S, $\ce{Sn^2+}$ to $\ce{Sn^4+}$; orange → green.

**KMnO₄ preparation:** $\ce{2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 -> 2K2MnO4 + 2H2O}$; manganate (green, $d^1$, paramagnetic) disproportionates in acid, $\ce{3MnO4^2- + 4H+ -> 2MnO4- + MnO2 + 2H2O}$, or is oxidised electrolytically. Permanganate is purple, tetrahedral, diamagnetic (colour from charge transfer).

**Oxidising action:** acid $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$ ($E^\circ$ +1.52 V) — oxidises $\ce{Fe^2+}$, oxalate, iodide; it is a self-indicator. Neutral/faintly alkaline $\ce{MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-}$, e.g. iodide → iodate. Do not acidify with HCl (chloride is oxidised).

**Titration ratios:** $\ce{Cr2O7^2-} : \ce{Fe^2+} = 1 : 6$; $\ce{MnO4-} : \ce{Fe^2+} = 1 : 5$; $\ce{MnO4-} : \ce{C2O4^2-} = 2 : 5$.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced.
A titrant whose own colour marks the end point, as permanganate does.

sections.heading: 4. Lanthanoids and actinoids
sections.body_md:
**Lanthanoids** (Ce–Lu) fill 4f: $[\text{Xe}]4f^{1\text{–}14}5d^{0\text{–}1}6s^2$. Common oxidation state **+3**; $\ce{Ce^4+}$ ($4f^0$) is an oxidant, $\ce{Eu^2+}$ ($4f^7$) and $\ce{Yb^2+}$ ($4f^{14}$) are reductants. Only promethium is radioactive.

**Lanthanoid contraction:** steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu, due to the imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another. **Consequences:** 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost identical radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) and properties, so they are hard to separate; basicity of $\ce{Ln(OH)3}$ decreases from La to Lu; lanthanoids are hard to separate from each other.

**Actinoids** (Th–Lr) fill 5f. 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close and 5f orbitals extend further than 4f, so actinoids show **more oxidation states** (up to +7 for Np, Pu), a **greater actinoid contraction**, more complex formation, and **all are radioactive**.

key_terms.definition_md: The steady decrease in size of lanthanoid atoms and ions with increasing atomic number, due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.

visual.caption: Approximate values: the steady decrease is the lanthanoid contraction.

sections.heading: 5. Applications of d- and f-block elements
sections.body_md:
- **Iron and steels:** construction; **stainless steel** (Fe with Cr and Ni) resists corrosion.
- **Titanium:** light, strong alloys for aircraft and medical implants.
- **Catalysts:** $\ce{V2O5}$ (contact process), Fe (Haber process), Ni (hydrogenation of oils), $\ce{TiCl4}$ with $\ce{Al(CH3)3}$ (Ziegler catalyst for polythene), $\ce{PdCl2}$ (Wacker process).
- **Coinage and electrical metals:** Cu, Ag, Au; **AgBr** in photography.
- **Mischmetall:** about 95% lanthanoid metals with about 5% iron (and traces of S, C, Ca, Al) — lighter flints, alloys.
- **Lanthanoid oxides:** phosphors in screens and lamps.
- **Actinoids:** uranium and plutonium as nuclear fuels.

key_terms.definition_md: An alloy of lanthanoid metals with about 5% iron, used in lighter flints.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when writing configurations of ions.
- Calling zinc a transition element, or forgetting that copper is one (Cu²⁺ is d⁹).
- Writing that permanganate's purple colour is a d–d transition (it is charge transfer; Mn is d⁰).
- Saying chromate → dichromate is a redox change (Cr is +6 in both).
- Forgetting the 1 : 6 and 1 : 5 ratios in dichromate and permanganate titrations.
- Giving the lanthanoid contraction without its cause (poor 4f shielding) or a consequence (Zr–Hf).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, configuration, oxidation state or colour.
- Reasoning (2–3 marks): the fact (1) + the configuration-based reason (1) + an example or consequence (1).
- Equations: correct species (½–1) + balanced atoms and charge (½–1).
- 5-mark answers: preparation with equations, structure, and two or three reactions; or contraction with cause and consequences.

questions.stem_md: The electronic configuration of Co²⁺ (Co, Z = 27) is:

options.text_md: $[\text{Ar}]3d^7$
$[\text{Ar}]3d^9$

questions.solution_md: Co is $[\text{Ar}]3d^7 4s^2$. The two 4s electrons are removed first, giving $[\text{Ar}]3d^7$ — option (a). (b) removes 3d electrons instead of 4s.

questions.stem_md: Chromium (Z = 24) has the configuration [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ instead of [Ar]3d⁴4s². The best explanation is:

options.text_md: a half-filled 3d subshell is extra stable, and the 3d and 4s energies are very close
4s orbitals are higher in energy than 4p orbitals
chromium has only one valence electron
the 3d subshell can hold only five electrons

questions.solution_md: Exchange energy makes the half-filled d⁵ arrangement especially stable, and since 3d and 4s are close in energy, one electron shifts — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Zinc is not regarded as a transition element.

**Reason (R):** Zinc has a completely filled d subshell both in its ground state and in its common oxidation state.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. A transition element needs an incomplete d subshell in the atom or a common ion; Zn (3d¹⁰4s²) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) have none, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Copper is regarded as a transition element even though the copper atom has a completely filled 3d subshell.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Its common ion Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, an incompletely filled d subshell.

questions.stem_md: In the ground state of a copper atom, the 3d subshell contains ___ electrons.
questions.solution_md: Copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹: the 3d subshell holds **10** electrons, because a filled 3d subshell is extra stable.

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configurations of Mn²⁺ (Z = 25) and Fe³⁺ (Z = 26). Why is Fe³⁺ more stable than Fe²⁺ in air?

answer.model_answer_md: Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵: both have a half-filled 3d subshell. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) is easily oxidised by air to Fe³⁺, because losing the sixth d electron gives the extra-stable half-filled d⁵ arrangement.

questions.solution_md: Remove 4s electrons first; link stability to the half-filled d⁵ configuration.

questions.stem_md: Which element of the 3d series shows the highest oxidation state?

options.text_md: Iron
Chromium
Zinc
Manganese

questions.solution_md: Manganese uses all seven 3d and 4s electrons to reach +7 (as in permanganate); after Mn, pairing of d electrons lowers the maximum — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which ion is both colourless in aqueous solution and diamagnetic?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{Sc^3+}$ is $3d^0$: no unpaired electron and no d–d transition — option (c). $\ce{Ti^3+}$ ($d^1$), $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ($d^9$) and $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ($d^5$) have unpaired electrons and are coloured.

questions.stem_md: Enthalpies of atomisation (kJ mol⁻¹): vanadium 515, chromium 397, iron 416, zinc 126. Which statement best explains the very low value for zinc?

options.text_md: Zinc has the largest number of unpaired d electrons in the series.
Zinc has no unpaired d electrons, so only its 4s electrons take part in metallic bonding.
Zinc atoms are much heavier than vanadium atoms.
Zinc has an incompletely filled 3d subshell.

questions.solution_md: Unpaired d electrons strengthen metallic bonding. Zinc is 3d¹⁰4s²: its d electrons are all paired and not used, so bonding, and the enthalpy of atomisation, are lowest — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Metallic radii (pm): Fe 126, Co 125, Ni 125, Cu 128. A student expected the radius to fall steadily because the nuclear charge rises by one each time. Which statement best explains the data?

options.text_md: Each added electron enters the 4s orbital, which increases the size.
Each added electron enters the inner 3d subshell; its weak shielding is balanced by repulsion between d electrons, so the size hardly changes.
The nuclear charge of these elements is the same.
These metals have different crystal structures, so their radii cannot be compared.

questions.solution_md: The rise in nuclear charge is largely offset by the screening and mutual repulsion of the added 3d electrons, so radii stay nearly constant (and rise slightly at Cu, 3d¹⁰) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Pieces of zinc, iron, nickel and copper are dropped into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. $E^\circ(\ce{M^2+/M})$: Zn $-0.76$, Fe $-0.44$, Ni $-0.25$, Cu $+0.34\ \text{V}$. Which metal gives no bubbles of hydrogen, and why?

options.text_md: Copper, because its E° is positive, so it cannot reduce H⁺ ions to hydrogen
Zinc, because its E° is the most negative
Nickel, because its E° is closest to zero
Iron, because it forms a protective oxide layer in acid

questions.solution_md: Only metals with negative E°(M²⁺/M) can reduce H⁺ to H₂. Copper (+0.34 V) cannot: the energy to atomise and ionise copper is not repaid by the hydration of Cu²⁺ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: $E^\circ(\ce{Mn^3+/Mn^2+}) = +1.57\ \text{V}$ while $E^\circ(\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+}) = -0.41\ \text{V}$. Which statement follows?

options.text_md: $\ce{Mn^3+}$ is a reducing agent and $\ce{Cr^2+}$ is an oxidising agent.
Both are strong oxidising agents.
Both are stable and unreactive in water.
$\ce{Mn^3+}$ is a strong oxidising agent and $\ce{Cr^2+}$ is a reducing agent.

questions.solution_md: A large positive $E^\circ$ means $\ce{Mn^3+}$ readily gains an electron (forming stable $d^5$ $\ce{Mn^2+}$); a negative $E^\circ$ means $\ce{Cr^2+}$ readily loses one (forming stable $d^3$ $\ce{Cr^3+}$) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which ion has the highest spin-only magnetic moment? (Z: Mn 25, Fe 26, Ni 28, Cu 29)
questions.solution_md: Unpaired electrons: $\ce{Mn^2+}$ ($d^5$) 5, $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($d^6$) 4, $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($d^8$) 2, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ($d^9$) 1. Most unpaired electrons gives the highest μ (5.92 BM) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the contact process, vanadium pentoxide oxidises sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide and is itself reduced to V₂O₄, which is then reoxidised by air back to V₂O₅. Which property of transition metals does this best illustrate?

options.text_md: Their high melting points
Their ability to form interstitial compounds
Their ability to change oxidation state easily, which makes them good catalysts
Their paramagnetism

questions.solution_md: Vanadium cycles between +5 and +4, forming and regenerating an intermediate: variable oxidation states make it a catalyst — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Dissolving a small amount of carbon in iron gives steel that is much harder than pure iron and still conducts electricity. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: carbon reacts with iron to form an ionic carbide that does not conduct
carbon replaces iron atoms one for one, since they are the same size
small carbon atoms occupy holes in the iron lattice, forming an interstitial compound that resists slipping of the layers
carbon removes the unpaired d electrons of iron

questions.solution_md: Carbon atoms fit into lattice holes (interstitial compound): the metal stays metallic and conducting but becomes harder and higher melting — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Salts of zinc are white, and their solutions are colourless.

**Reason (R):** Zn²⁺ has an incompletely filled 3d subshell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, a completely filled subshell, so no d–d transition is possible — which is why its salts are colourless — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cr²⁺ is a strong oxidising agent.

**Reason (R):** $E^\circ(\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+})$ is negative ($-0.41\ \text{V}$).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the negative potential means Cr²⁺ readily loses an electron to become Cr³⁺, so it is a reducing agent. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Transition metals form alloys with each other very easily.

**Reason (R):** Transition metals generally have high densities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but alloys form readily because the atoms have similar radii and can replace one another in the lattice, not because of density — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment, in BM, of Ni²⁺ (Ni, Z = 28).
questions.solution_md: $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$, so $n = 2$ unpaired electrons. $\mu = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$, in BM.

questions.stem_md: A 3d metal ion has a spin-only magnetic moment of 5.92 BM. How many unpaired electrons does it have?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$, so $n(n+2) = 5.92^2 \approx 35.0$.

Step 2 — Solving $n^2 + 2n - 35 = 0$: $\sqrt{4 + 140} = 12$, so $n = (-2 + 12) \div 2 = 5$ (check: $5 \times 7 = 35$). So the ion has 5 unpaired electrons (for example $\ce{Mn^2+}$ or $\ce{Fe^3+}$).

questions.stem_md: What is the oxidation state of chromium in the dichromate ion, $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$? (Give the number.)

$E^\circ(\ce{M^2+/M})$ values are: Mn $-1.18\ \text{V}$, Fe $-0.44\ \text{V}$, Zn $-0.76\ \text{V}$, Cu $+0.34\ \text{V}$. Explain why the value for manganese is more negative than expected from the general trend, and why copper’s is positive.

answer.model_answer_md: Mn²⁺ has a half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, which is extra stable, so manganese forms Mn²⁺ more readily and its E° is more negative. For copper, the high enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation needed to make Cu²⁺(aq) is not compensated by its hydration enthalpy, so E° is positive.

questions.solution_md: d⁵ stability for Mn; energy balance of atomisation, ionisation and hydration for Cu.

marking_scheme.step: Mn: stable half-filled d⁵ of Mn²⁺
Cu: atomisation + ionisation not compensated by hydration

questions.stem_md: Why does the number of oxidation states in the 3d series increase up to manganese and then decrease?

answer.model_answer_md: Up to manganese, all 3d and 4s electrons can be used in bonding, so the highest oxidation state rises from +3 (Sc) to +7 (Mn). After manganese, the d electrons begin to pair; paired electrons are harder to use, so fewer oxidation states are shown and the maximum falls to +2 at zinc.

questions.solution_md: Number of available unpaired d electrons rises to Mn, then pairing reduces it.

marking_scheme.step: Up to Mn all (n − 1)d and ns electrons can be used
After Mn pairing reduces the number of usable electrons

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts, with one industrial example for each reason.

answer.model_answer_md: First, they show variable oxidation states, so they can form unstable intermediates and then regenerate, as V₂O₅ does in the contact process for sulfuric acid. Second, they provide surfaces that adsorb reactant molecules and weaken their bonds, as iron does in the Haber process and nickel in the hydrogenation of oils.

questions.solution_md: Variable oxidation states; surface adsorption.

marking_scheme.step: Variable oxidation states with an example

questions.stem_md: Explain why most transition metal ions are coloured in solution. Use your explanation to predict whether Ti⁴⁺, V³⁺ and Cu⁺ ions will be coloured. (Z: Ti 22, V 23, Cu 29)

answer.model_answer_md: In a hydrated ion the five d orbitals split into sets of slightly different energy. An electron in a partly filled d subshell absorbs visible light of a particular energy to jump to a higher d orbital (a d–d transition), and the solution shows the complementary colour. Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰ and Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transition is possible: both are colourless. V³⁺ is 3d², so it is coloured (green).

questions.solution_md: Partly filled d subshell gives d–d transitions; d⁰ and d¹⁰ do not.

marking_scheme.step: Explanation: d–d transition absorbs visible light, complementary colour seen
Ti⁴⁺ d⁰ and Cu⁺ d¹⁰ colourless

questions.stem_md: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moments of Ti³⁺, Mn²⁺ and Zn²⁺ (Z: Ti 22, Mn 25, Zn 30). Which of them is diamagnetic, and which is likely to be colourless?

answer.model_answer_md:
Ti³⁺ is $3d^1$: $n = 1$, $\mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ BM. Mn²⁺ is $3d^5$: $n = 5$, $\mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM. Zn²⁺ is $3d^{10}$: $n = 0$, $\mu = 0$.

Zn²⁺ is diamagnetic, and with a full d subshell it has no d–d transition, so it is colourless.

questions.solution_md: Find n from the d count, then μ = √(n(n + 2)).

marking_scheme.step: Zn²⁺ diamagnetic and colourless with reason

questions.stem_md: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to a yellow solution of potassium chromate. What is observed, and why?

options.text_md: It turns green as chromium is reduced to +3.
It turns orange as dichromate forms; chromium stays in the +6 state.
It turns colourless as chromium is oxidised to +7.
No change, because chromate does not react with acid.

questions.solution_md: $\ce{2CrO4^2- + 2H+ <=> Cr2O7^2- + H2O}$: an acid–base change, not redox; Cr is +6 in both ions — option (b).

questions.stem_md: How many electrons does one permanganate ion gain when it acts as an oxidising agent in acidic solution?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons — option (d). (a) is the neutral-solution value.

questions.stem_md: A few drops of an unknown colourless liquid are warmed with acidified potassium dichromate solution, and the orange colour turns green. What can you conclude?

options.text_md: The liquid is an oxidising agent; it has oxidised chromium from +3 to +6.
The liquid is a reducing agent; it has reduced chromium from +6 to +3.
The liquid is an alkali; it has turned dichromate into chromate.
No reaction occurred; the colour change is due to warming.

questions.solution_md: Green Cr³⁺ forms only when Cr₂O₇²⁻ (Cr +6) is reduced, so the liquid gave electrons — option (b). Alkali (c) would give yellow chromate, not green.

questions.stem_md: In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, potassium permanganate oxidises iodide ions. The manganese-containing product is:

options.text_md: manganese(II) ions, $\ce{Mn^2+}$
manganate ions, $\ce{MnO4^2-}$
manganese dioxide, $\ce{MnO2}$
manganese metal

questions.solution_md: In neutral solution $\ce{MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-}$; brown $\ce{MnO2}$ forms and iodide is oxidised to iodate — option (c). $\ce{Mn^2+}$ (a) forms in acid.

questions.stem_md: No separate indicator is added in titrations of iron(II) with potassium permanganate because:

options.text_md: the first excess drop of permanganate gives a permanent pink colour, since Mn²⁺ is almost colourless
iron(III) ions are deep purple
permanganate turns colourless only at the end point
the reaction gives off a gas at the end point

questions.solution_md: Before the end point, purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to nearly colourless Mn²⁺ at once; one extra drop stays pink — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In $\ce{3MnO4^2- + 4H+ -> 2MnO4- + MnO2 + 2H2O}$, the oxidation state of manganese changes:

options.text_md: from +7 to +6 and +4
from +6 to +7 only
from +6 to +7 and +4
from +4 to +6 and +7

questions.solution_md: Manganate (+6) is both oxidised to permanganate (+7) and reduced to MnO₂ (+4): a disproportionation — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Permanganate titrations are not carried out in the presence of hydrochloric acid.

**Reason (R):** Permanganate oxidises chloride ions to chlorine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Potassium chloride is added: Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl, and the less soluble orange crystals separate. Chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing one oxygen (Cr–O–Cr about 126°). In acid, chromate changes to dichromate; in alkali, the reverse: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O; Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6I⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O.

The length of the green band showed how much ethanol had been breathed out. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) +6 to +3

**(b)** 1.38 mg

**(c)** (i) The equation needs eight hydrogen ions for each dichromate ion: in acid, dichromate is a strong oxidising agent and is reduced to Cr³⁺. Without acid it could not oxidise the ethanol, and the colour change would not occur.

**OR** (ii) Purple permanganate would be reduced to almost colourless manganese(II), so the purple colour would fade. $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Cr is +6 in dichromate and +3 in Cr³⁺: it is reduced, while ethanol is oxidised — option (c).

**(b)** Ratio 3 ethanol : 1 dichromate, so ethanol $= 3 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-5} = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}$ mol. Molar mass of ethanol $= 46$. Mass $= 3.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 46 = 0.00138$ g, that is $0.00138 \times 1000 = 1.38$ mg.

**(c)** (i) H⁺ is a reactant; dichromate oxidises strongly only in acid.

(ii) Permanganate in acid: purple to colourless.
